summary: A superconducting quantum controller fabricated in Nb on high-resistivity silicon achieves 99.9% average Clifford fidelity with $10^{-4}$-level leakage when integrated at 10 mK with a transmon qubit, using single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulse trains for all-digital qubit control. The device combines a fully passive bias network and spectrum-engineering unit to suppress quasiparticle poisoning and high-energy-level leakage, operating at an average gate energy of 0.121 fJ with negligible thermal load.
motivation: Superconducting quantum computing faces a control bottleneck due to wiring complexity, heat load, and decoherence when operating room-temperature electronics at millikelvin temperatures; cryogenic superconducting control schemes promise low power and high speed but have not yet matched room-temperature electronics performance.
method: The controller uses SFQ pulse trains with frequency $\omega_{\mathrm{SQC}} \approx \omega_{01}/2$ as a noise-immune digital drive, employs a passive superconducting bias network and low-critical-current topology to minimize quasiparticle generation, integrates spectrum engineering to filter high-frequency harmonics and reduce leakage, and connects directly to qubits via coaxial cables at the 10 mK stage of a dilution refrigerator.
result: Randomized benchmarking yields uniformly high gate fidelities (99.90(1)% average Clifford, 99.90(2)% for $X^{\pi/2}_{\mathrm{SQC}}$) with leakage $L_{\mathrm{SQC}} = 2.90 \times 10^{-4}$ per Clifford, decoherence-limited error $r^{\mathrm{cliff}}_{\mathrm{dec}} = 8.91 \times 10^{-4}$, and baseline qubit excited-state population $P_e = (4.76 \pm 0.49)\%$ indicating $T_{\mathrm{eff}} = 78.3 \pm 2.8$ mK with no measurable controller-induced heating.
